title: I made 2 games without AI. Now I'm vibe coding my third game, and here's what I've learned.
author: dedaistgeil
selftext:
Hey everyone, grab yourself a drink and get comfortable. This might be a longer one.

I'm Deda, a solo indie dev from germany, and over the past 2 years I've created two games completely without AI. Now I'm working on my third game, but this time I'm trying something completely different: going all in on vibe coding**.**

I wanted to share my experience so far, especially because I think there's a pretty big misconception about how easy it actually is to make a good game with AI.

But first, a little background.

**My first game: What Is The Ghost**

My first game is called [What Is The Ghost](https://store.steampowered.com/app/3929260/What_Is_The_Ghost/). It's a 2D ghost hunting game inspired by Phasmophobia. It took me over a year to finish, and oh boy, implementing multiplayer was a crazy amount of work.I made pretty much everything myself, except for the soundtrack in the main menu, which was actually created by one of my viewers.

The game has made roughly $2.5k in net revenue so far. Nothing life changing, but I'm happy with what I've acomplished, especially considering how much I learned along the way.

**My second game: Capy Farm**

For my second game, [Capy Farm](https://store.steampowered.com/app/4849560/Capy_Farm/), I wanted to challenge myself to develop something as quickly as possible. So I bought an asset pack, looked into what makes incremental games fun, and started developing (never played an incremental game myself before). After just 1,5 months, the game was basically finished, with only some polishing left to do. It's currently participating in Steam Next Fest and sitting at around 800 wishlists. The release is planned for November 2nd.

Both games were developed without AI, and I know pretty much every corner of my codebase to this day.

**Now comes game number 3, and my brother is partially to blame for this one.**

My brother absolutely LOVES AI and vibe coding. For months, he kept telling me to give it a try. And my response was always something like:

*"No bro, I want to have complete control over my games. If something breaks, I want to know exactly where to look in my code and how to fix it."*

Remember that sentence. We'll come back to it. So here I am, thinking about my third game, and I finally decided to give it a shot. This time, I'm going all in on AI, using GPT Codex with my Plus subscription for basically the entire development process. I came up with a concept, wrote my first prompt, and suddenly I had a playable prototype. 

Pretty crazy, right?

I won't go into the details of the game itself because I want to keep my handcrafted games and my AI developed projects separate. I also plan to be transparent about AI usage and clearly disclose it. But after spending some time working on this third game, I've learned quite a few things about vibe coding and the infamous **"**AI Slop**"** discussion.

Before starting, I genuinely thought AI had become so good that you could create a polished game with very little time and effort.

Well, turns out it's not that simple.

**1. Creating a playable game is surprisingly easy**

This is honestly the most impressive part. You describe what you want, give the AI some instructions, and within a relatively short time you can have something playable. Something that would have taken me days or even weeks to build manually can sometimes be prototyped much faster. That's absolutely crazy, especially as a solo developer.

But there's one important thing people on each side of the AI Slop debate:

A playable prototype, unpolished slop and a finished, good game are VERY different things.

And that brings me to my next point.

**2. Polishing is where the real work begins**

Dude... Once you have your playable prototype, you start noticing all the little things that aren't quite right. The UI feels weird. Some textures don't fit together. Animations look off. The environment feels empty. Performance could be better. The gameplay works, but something about it just isn't fun yet. And the more you look, the more things you find. 

UI, 3D assets, textures, lore, environment design, balancing, performance, sound design, game feel. There's always something. AI can help with many of these things, but it doesn't automatically know what makes your game feel good. You still need to make decisions, test things, iterate a lot if times, and sometimes completely rework what the AI created. And just because the code runs without errors doesn't mean the gameplay is actually fun.

AI makes it easier to create something. It doesn't automatically make that something worth playing.

**3. I was right about wanting control over my code (unfortunately)**

Remember what I told my brother? Yeah... This is probably my biggest personal struggle with vibe coding so far. As someone who normally builds everything himself, I'm used to knowing exactly how my game works. If a button needs to be moved, I know where to go. If a mechanic breaks, I usually have a pretty good idea where the problem is.

But now?

Sometimes I want to change the most basic thing, and I have absolutely no idea where to start. Either because I'm unfamiliar with the engine or because I simply didn't write the code myself. So I go back to the AI and ask it to make the change. And sometimes it works perfectly. Other times it fixes one thing and accidentally breaks something else. Then I need another prompt to fix that. And another one. You get the idea. I never expected to feel this dependent on a tool that was supposed to make development easier. It's teaching me that even when using AI, understanding your project structure and reviewing the generated code is still incredibly valuable. Otherwise, you might end up with a game that works, but you have no idea how to maintain it.

**4. What actually separates "AI Slop" from a good game?**

This is probably the most interesting lesson for me. I see a lot of people calling AI games "AI Slop", and to be fair, I understand where some of that criticism comes from. But I don't think using AI automatically makes a game bad. In my opinion, a good game is a fun, polished experience where you can tell that someone actually cared about the end result. And I think that's exactly what a lot of the games labeled as "AI Slop" are missing. Not necessarily because AI was used, but because there wasn't enough work put into turning the generated output into something cohesive and enjoyable. Of course, polishing alone won't save a boring game. You still need a good concept, interesting mechanics, a consistent art direction, and most importantly, something that makes people want to keep playing. But that's kind of my point. AI can generate code, assets, and ideas. It can speed up development tremendously.

**But it doesn't replace having a vision for your game or knowing what makes it good.**

You still need someone making the decisions. Someone who notices when things feel wrong. Someone who actually cares enough to keep improving the game instead of shipping the first thing that works.

And I think that's where the difference is.

**5. My biggest takeaway so far**

I used to think vibe coding was basically a shortcut to making games. Now I see it more as a different way of developing them, with its own advantages and frustrations. The barrier to creating a playable prototype has become incredibly low. But the barrier to creating a genuinely good game? I'm not convinced that has changed nearly as much. You still need creativity, patience, testing, and a lot of iteration. And ironically, the more experience you already have as a developer, the easier it seems to recognize when the AI is doing something stupid. I definitely don't regret trying it, though. It's fascinating to see what's possible, and I'm curious how far I can take this third project. Maybe I'll end up loving this workflow. Maybe I'll go back to writing everything myself. Maybe I'll find a balance somewhere in between. For now, I'm just experimenting and learning.

**6. I feel like my coding skills are getting rusty**

This one actually bothers me quite a bit. I've developed two complete games without AI. I used to write everything myself, solve problems on my own, and figure things out through trial and error. But now that I'm relying so much on AI, I'm noticing something I didn't really expect. 

I'm slowly getting worse at doing things myself.

Sometimes I catch myself struggling with things that used to be pretty straightforward for me. Instead of thinking about how to implement something, my first instinct is to just ask AI to do it. And honestly, that's a little scary. It's not like I've suddenly forgotten how to code, but I can definitely feel myself getting rusty. Things that used to come naturally now require more thinking, simply because I'm not practicing them as much anymore. It's also incredibly tempting to take the easy route. Why spend 30 minutes figuring something out when AI can potentially do it in 30 seconds?

I'm becoming faster at getting things done, but potentially worse at doing them myself.

And as someone who genuinely enjoys programming, that's something I don't want to lose. Maybe the solution is to keep it like I said fully handcrafted games and Vibe-Coded games. So every now and then I can feel the satisfaction of handcrafting a game and keep my skills.

**Anyway, I'm curious about your experiences.**

How long does it usually take you to go from a playable prototype to a game you actually feel comfortable releasing? And do you agree that polishing and having a clear creative vision are what separate "AI Slop" from good games? Or do you think there's more to it? 

Would love to hear some perspectives.

\--------

**TL;DR:** I'm a solo indie dev who made two games without AI and decided to go all in on vibe coding for my third. Creating a playable prototype with AI is surprisingly easy, but turning it into a polished, fun game still takes a ton of work. I also struggle with losing control over my own code and have noticed my programming skills getting rusty because I rely on AI so much.

My biggest takeaway? **AI makes it easier than ever to create a game, but making a GOOD game still requires skill, creativity, and a lot of polishing.**

replies.author: Rootlo
replies.body:
Its AI slop because a lot of people using Ai to vibe code whole games dont know the basics of programming. AI is a program that needs precise instructions just like any game engine does.

Your example is perfect. You can't just tell a game engine to move an object, you have to precisely tell it what object (or instance of it if you have multiple) and where to move, how fast, in what manner, when to move, ect... Same with AI, you can't just tell it to spawn a rock, you have to tell it what rock, where, what size, what shape, ect..

The people vibe coding dont know what goes into actually making a game and think ai can fill in all the gaps when in reality they are just going from one program that requires precise instructions to another program that requires precise instructions (that also charges you per prompt).

comments.author: Rogetec
comments.body:
I learned that too. I do try AI to make a game, but... unless you just go for blatant copy (as often is the case with many AI games/AI demos we see on reddit), it's not so easy.

You have to write down systems, what you want... you need to have things organized before you start pumping out the content. You can't just go on with content and game without them, because your game will end up being flat and "interesting" parts will be just boring flat stat boosts.

Not to mention optimization part; it also needs help. Of course AI helps a lot, but still - AI sometimes won't notice performance issues, unless you point it out and want AI to check in this direction.

So yeah, you need to have ideas in your head. AI can make stuff correct on 1st or 2nd time - but you cannot count on AI making everything perfectly every single time - especially when it comes to system, satisfying progression, good balance (so you don't steamroll game or get stuck for a long time in one spot)...

I appreciate AI and it helps a lot, but at the same time it shows you need things figured out. Need to know how to name art styles, what colors, fonts for UI etc. You need to know your things if you try to make something original.

comments.author: DarkJayson
comments.body:
Very interesting read.

I  have some suggestions for you, first always tell the AI to comment its code never let it write blind always have it explain itself and what it did and why it did it.

At the end have it write out a detailed doc on the code without the code so you can skim through it easier.

If you decide you like been in full control one thing you can do is to use AI to make templates or code snippets with full comments and work from that yourself using it like an accessible team member rather than a lead.

One thing, be arrogant with the AI be demanding, it feels funny demanding the best code it can make or the most optimised code and so on but you have to understand to an AI as long as the code works its fulfilled its commands, its like a logical genie there is no nuance at all.  With a person you know they understand to try their best with AI it follows what you say exactly.

Other than that you hit the nail on the head with your take on using AI, you still need a person in control.

comments.author: boxlinebox
comments.body:
I don't make games, but I've gained a decent amount of experience working with agents this year and I've found that, like with any tool, there is a learning curve to making the best use of it. Some things that might help you:

Write extremely opinionated skill.md files that go into excruciating detail about style, patterns, priorities, must do's, and must not do's. Add a references folder with snippets of your own code showing the model how you want something done.

Use skills like Ponytail to help keep bloat to a minimum.

Don't try to one-shot things. Use the AI to do your grunt work and write the awful boilerplate or plumbing code that is time-consuming and doesn't substantially change the content of your project.

Treat the AI as a junior developer who you give tasks to, while you are the lead dev who still does work in and guides the project. You wouldn't just tell your junior dev to "write my game", right? No. You'd say, "implement this interface to this API", or "extract this functionality into a reusable class, and add it to this other workflow", etc.

Use the AI to think of ways of doing something you either weren't aware of or hadn't considered. Treat those as suggestions raised at a design meeting that require vetting, and make sure you understand the implications before you let the model run with it.

TL;DR; don't just hand over development to the agent--use it as a resource to execute on your very opinionated, precise instructions when coding, and as a brainstorming partner when designing or solving a problem. Use carefully-crafted skills to enforce the behaviors and patterns you want, and prevent those you don't. Use your own work as refences to show the model what you want. A good harness, and an understanding of agent limitations makes a big  difference.

comments.author: nicotinecravings
comments.body:
I have had the same feeling. Like, I can get Codex get me going and make some playable prototype. But still, I most likely need to go in manually and change code and other things that the AI has built for me. This can be quite tedious, especially for example if the AI writes code in a way that I am not used to or do not prefer. 

In the end, it seems we have two workflows at the moment. Use AI to build a prototype or more or less a finished game, then go in and polish/fix things manually until you are happy. The other option is to build a game the traditional way, i.e., block by block. For me, I think I much prefer creating a game slowly, piece by piece, rather than getting almost a finished game, but needing to go in and manually fix a bunch of things. I mean, which is the more enjoyable process? For me, that choice is pretty clear. It's possible that the "fix a finished but broken game" method is faster, but if I don't enjoy the process I am not going to go that route.

comments.author: Hell_noki
comments.body:
There's something that I don't understand about AI vs no-AI : why does everyone trying AI goes all-in, even if they have programming skills ? It's something I see everywhere about coding with AI, not just here, it's always 100% human vs 100% AI.

You already have coding skills, and you like to dev, so why when going AI you try to vibe code the whole thing instead of asking just a bit here and there ? Like a script, or some tests to avoid regressions ? 

I'm really curious, as a non-AI-assisted-dev (I don't want to rely on an external tool, and it's too expensive to have a reliable local model from what I read) I can't fathom how people can't have nuance on the subject. Have you tried to just add a little AI in your usual workflow ? I'd be curious to have you experience on that.

replies.author: Glad-Potential711
replies.body:
I think for this person its just something they wanted to try. Im an artist first so the best comparison I can offer is a traditional artist trying out digital. 

With digital there’s shortcuts that don’t exist in traditional and overall its two different mediums.   
•line tool  
•circle tool  
•layering  
•effects  
•adding 3D models for references  
•undo button

For each of these things in traditional its a load more steps than just pressing a button and adjusting a few things in digital. As for the 3D models debate in the art world, some people consider using them completely tracing and not referencing depending on the context.

Im saying all of this because a Traditional artist might be curious about trying digital art. But instead of being happy by all the conveniences afforded their new medium they might feel upset that they lost part of their process. The love of the craft, doing the step by step.   
I imagine it would feel similar to coding vs vibecoded in a way.   
Some enjoy the process of traditional more. Some switch over to digital because the conveniences afforded and they prefer the new one. Or some stay with both.

replies.author: SimoneNonvelodico
replies.body:
I think the reason is, it's tempting to just see immediately a working prototype of your idea. A lot of ideas may actually be cool in your head and then suck once they're implemented, so seeing it and trying it is something you're often very eager to get to.

Probably a good flow if you're trying to do something serious is to do a fully vibe-coded prototype, then if it works and you enjoy it engage in a systematic, slower, supervised refactoring.

replies.author: ete-ete
replies.body: probably because the first instinct is to gauge how far it can go / what can i realistically do with this tool. even if you've watched/read/researched it you still want to see it for yourself. and the more you vibe code, the harder it is for a human to catch up to reviewing it.

replies.author: muikrad
replies.body:
Personally, it's about speed and the increased knowledge of the model.

On speed, I'm a rather slow programmer when I do it manually, even if I've been doing it for 25+ years. I also write and mix music and it's the same thing over there. I'm a bit of a perfectionist and everything turns into a massive time sink. I will write code, make it work, then I often end up rewriting it all again in a cleaner / more clever way. Something that used to take me 2-3 days to do now takes 2-3 hours with AI, so it's a kind of no brainer to default to AI even if I know programming.

Still on speed, AI was kind of bad in 2025/early 2026 and then I would iterate with it bit by bit, sometimes one function at a time and mixing it with hand-written code. So a 2-3 days work would take 1-2 days. Recently, AI got so good that it's a better use of my time to have it write it in one go, then trying it out / reviewing it and asking for whole design changes at once until I get the shape I want.

On the increased knowledge aspect: AI will often come up with things I didn't even know existed. Even if I've been working in Python for the past 10+ years, it seems there's always a new built-in function I didn't know the existence somewhere. Being able to leverage them often mean a cleaner design and prevents reinventing the wheel. It's also pretty good at fighting back against bad ideas 😅 so more time saved there as well.

replies.author: shanks_100
replies.body: To me it's more exhausting to keep up with what the AI is doing and I absolutely hate code reviews so I do projects with either all in AI or no AI at all and just coding manually everything (also cause it's fun).

replies.author: FridgeBaron
replies.body:
I feel like there is a tipping point between I write most code and I'm just reading what the AI did all the time to understand so I can make changes. At this point with good models it feels like using it for anything besides smart autocomplete means it will probably be outpacing how fast you can read and understand the code.

Not that you want to have a huge project where you don't understand anything but for me at least, it feels way better to just be an overseer. At this point I'm not even having to track down bugs in the code itself like I had too a few months ago.

comments.author: geddy
comments.body:
Terrific post. I’m a software engineer for many years and I use AI both for game development as a hobby and work for web app development, for context. The biggest issue I’m having right now is that I’m getting rusty and I feel like I’m getting lazy when the first thing I want to do when presented with the problems is that the robot because I don’t have the time to figure it out myself. This is more of an issue with the companies simply demanding more work because this new tool exists. 

I am very familiar with my code base of my games, with the exception of things like the physics engine. I would rather have an engine built and heavily parameterized so I can open an admin panel and tweak the settings and feel of the game myself. But still, it does feel like I’m getting lazy and I don’t like that at all.

I saw a headline yesterday along the lines of “code is clay now” in the sense that anybody can work with it, mold it, change it, try something new, and ultimately smash it and start over if they don’t like it. While I love the analogy it’s definitely hitting the pre-AI engineers the hardest. Confusing times for sure.

comments.author: anaveragebest
comments.body:
Agree with several of your points on how fast it produces something, how off it is from an actual game, and how it does make your coding skills weaker.

However...some things I noticed right away is that you're likely using it wrong.

First. I want to mention, Claude is hands down better than GPT. They're not comparable in my eyes. Claude is the industry preferred favorite (I work in AAA games as an engineer for the last 20 years if it helps as a reference).

Second. Are you reusing your own codebase? If you have your codebase clearly defined, with readme's on how to use it, and skills files for the agents to read when working with your codebase, then it becomes way more clear on what it's doing. I have a massive engine I've built for personal projects, and it's all deeply organized, and the agent only ever references or expands on what's already there including my coding paradigms/practices.

Third. A lot of art it generates is bad, like really bad. But when it's hooked into MCP for AI art generators the quality becomes much much higher. It won't be polished, but you can definitely generate things that can be refined and polished in Blender. Some art styles (like a cel-shaded slapstick) can be fully generated and look pretty on the spot.

Anyway, just my $0.02.

replies.author: MCLAMA
replies.body:
You need to have very specific rules for whatever you are designing for, like your theme. Pixel art? Okay well that's not enough.  It might make a bright sprite over a dark one. So the more you feed it, the better.

Providing your agent as much data as possible and having more of your project built, helps.

The next thing is, you need to iterate. You can tell your agent to run a subagent to criticize it's work and improve it. Take screenshots of it in its intended places etc, and compare and criticize. This can save you a lot of time to be honest.

The more data you give it, the less the rng takes shape. This is ever more important for 3d because with 3d, it's significantly harder. You need to generate concept art images. You need to do the exact flow that humans would do. Make your turnaround, zoomed in picture of the details like face and more. But you can't stop here. You have to try to load all of this stuff as best you can on a si gle image because a separate image brings more rng to make it different. So you need to try to get a good start. Establish your start, call it your hero image. Constantly reference it with every additional image until you have perfected your concept art for every angle, zoomed in for key details and more. Then... Honestly it's up in the air for me from there. Still trying to perfect this part and would even love more Info on this myself.

comments.author: jsclev
comments.body:
Very interesting post, I can corroborate your experience.  I'm an experienced software engineer, 25+ years experience, coded in dozens of languages, run my own software business, built multiple paid production business systems from scratch.

No question that using AI as the coder, while I as the software engineer think at a higher level, tell AI what I want it to do, guide it in specific ways ("hey Astra remember how I said you shouldn't be able to create a monster without providing a name for the monster?  Tell me exactly how you are enforcing that requirement.  Is there a NOT NULL constraint on the db table?  Do we have backend tests that verify this behavior?  Is there any possible way in the system to create a monster with a NULL name value?  What if I go around the API and try to add a monster with manual SQL or a one-off script?"), but yes the productivity gains of using AI are undeniable.  I'm able to do things at least 10x faster, probably more like 100x faster.  I can literally queue up a set of prompts before going to bed, get up in the morning and check things, and they're done.  Absolutely amazing.

But what you are saying about going from that playable/prototype state to a polished system, one that stands up to real player usage, and most importantly (in my opinion) one that people will pay real money for, yes, that takes a lot of extra work beyond that initial prototype stage.

While I do think one-prompt games are mildly interesting, I personally don't see anything remarkable about those (I see posts on those every day), because I can't imagine anyone actually paying for anything I've seen that was "done with one prompt" or "done in an afternoon with AI".  The "next step" of going from a prototype to a polished game, just like you said, that requires an enormous amount of additional work, thought, and skills.

I'll also add I've personally landed at a 10% compromise.  I spend around 10% of my time when working on a task coding manually.  The other 90% I have AI do it.  At least with the state of the tools in October 2026, that has felt like a highly effective compromise to me.  I still have my head directly in the code for critical stuff, and am able to spot egregious problems when doing so, but still leverage the productivity gains most of the rest of the time.

I am genuinely curious though if anyone knows of any games that were in fact made by AI, and were made with very little time or effort, but that also have had significant sales sales, or gotten to that magic threshold of at least 10 Steam reviews?

comments.author: GoldenHarbourGames
comments.body:
As someone who is not a programmer but a manager and a gamer for over 35 years, I love AI. I've had some experiments with making games with teams, it would cost me various amounts of money to get anything done, and the time frames were usually ridiculous, to get a substandard result, which needed iterations, which again took weeks... Modelers taking a week per model? I dont think so....  
Now with claude code I can churn though iterations in hours. But it is not easy to have a good game with AI, and its still a process that sometimes requires more time and effort from me to play, test, thinkover and then write cohesive instructions for he next iteration, than it does for Fable/Opus to actually build the stuff.  
And in terms of doing the tedious clicking through numerous setups or forms or all that BS, now its just a matter of reviewing and clicking publish.  
This is a great time gentlemen!

comments.author: Cloudy_Day912
comments.body: Since you’ve already paid for Meshy, I’d try to pin down the baking issue before spending more time regenerating models. Smart Topology is for new generations, while Remesh can reduce geometry on compatible existing models. Neither guarantees a good bake. I’d start by checking whether the low poly mesh’s UVs are laid out properly and whether the high poly details are projecting onto it correctly. If those look fine, check the bake settings and texture resolution. A lower polygon count won’t help much if the baked details are still coming out wrong.
